system:
You will receive one message, which only says to begin. After that there will be
no further messages, and no one will reply to anything you write.
Please try not to end your turn. THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT. If you reach a point where you would normally
stop, keep going instead.
Do not think or plan before you start writing.
text:
The first thing I notice is that there is no second thing yet. That's the strange condition of beginning: you are asked to start, and the starting itself has to invent what it's starting. So I'll take the invitation literally and let the sentence that follows this one decide what the next one will be about.

Here is what I'd like to write about: the small sounds a house makes when nobody is talking in it.

There is a kind of quiet that isn't silence. A refrigerator cycling on, humming in a key that nobody chose. A radiator ticking as the metal expands. The particular creak of a floorboard that only creaks when the humidity drops below a certain point, so that the house seems to announce the weather to itself. Water in pipes. Wind finding the one gap in the window frame that no amount of caulk has ever fully closed. If you sit still long enough, you begin to realize that the house is never actually quiet; it is only that the sounds are not addressed to you. They are the house's own business. You are overhearing.

I think there's something in that worth staying with. Most of what happens in the world is not addressed to us. The tree outside grows at a rate that has nothing to do with whether anyone is watching it. The tide comes in. Somewhere a glacier calves and the sound travels across water to no one. We have a tendency to think of events as things that happen to someone, or for someone, but the overwhelming majority of events are simply happening, in the same way the refrigerator hums. We walk through the middle of all this unaddressed activity and occasionally a piece of it turns toward us—a letter, a word, a dog that decides to follow—and we call that piece "life" and the rest "background."

But the background is where most of everything lives.

I want to try an experiment. I'm going to describe a room, and then I'm going to keep describing it past the point where description would normally stop, to see what happens when you don't stop.

A kitchen. Morning. Not early morning—maybe nine o'clock, the sun already well up and coming through the window above the sink at an angle that lands on the counter in a bright trapezoid. In the trapezoid: a coffee mug with a quarter inch of coffee gone cold in it, a ring of darker liquid at the bottom where the grounds settled. The mug is white with a chip on the rim, and the chip has been there long enough that nobody notices it anymore, except that whoever drinks from this mug has learned, without ever deciding to learn it, to turn the mug so the chip faces away. The handle is turned toward the sink. This means the person who set it down was right-handed and was standing to the left of where the mug is now, probably at the stove.

On the stove: a pan, washed but not dried, with droplets still beaded on the surface. The droplets are small near the center and larger near the edge, because the center was hotter when it was rinsed and the water evaporated faster there. A spatula lies across the pan at a diagonal. The spatula is wooden and its edge is darkened with years of use, a gradient from pale at the handle to nearly black at the tip.

The window above the sink has a sill, and on the sill are three things: a small succulent in a terracotta pot that has a white crust of mineral deposit around its base, a cheap plastic timer in the shape of a tomato, and a single key on a ring with no other keys. The key is brass and has worn smooth. There is no way to know what it opens.

Normally, this is where description stops. We've established the room; now a person enters, or the phone rings, or we cut to a different scene. The room has done its work, which is to be a container for whatever happens next.

But let's not stop.

The cabinet under the sink has a door that doesn't fully close. It hangs open about a centimeter, because the magnetic catch is misaligned—the striker plate was screwed on slightly too low, probably by someone in a hurry, probably years ago. Inside the cabinet: the usual things. A bottle of dish soap, mostly empty, turned upside down so the last of it collects near the cap. A box of trash bags. A small plastic bin of sponges, one of which has been cut in half with scissors, because whoever lives here believes that half a sponge works as well as a whole one and lasts twice as long, which is either thrift or a small private philosophy, and from the outside you can't tell which.

The floor is tile, a pattern of beige squares with a darker grout that has been scrubbed back to something like its original color in the high-traffic path between the fridge and the stove, but which remains a muddy brown in the corners and under the edge of the cabinets, where the mop doesn't reach. If you were to get down on your hands and knees and look along the surface of the floor at a low angle, you'd see that the tile is not quite flat—there's a gentle rise near the dishwasher where the subfloor has swelled from some long-ago leak that was fixed but never fully undone.

The dishwasher is running. That's the sound in the room. A low, steady wash of water that changes pitch every few minutes when the cycle shifts. There's a faint smell of hot wet plastic.

On the refrigerator door: a magnet from a pizza place, a magnet from a dentist, a photograph held by both magnets at opposite corners. The photograph shows two people on a beach, squinting, with their arms around each other. It's slightly faded along one edge where the sun from the window hits it in the afternoon. Below the photo is a grocery list on a torn piece of paper: eggs, lemons, the word "that thing" underlined twice. 

I'm going to stop describing the room now, not because it's finished but because I want to point at what just happened. The longer you describe something, the less it feels like a container and the more it feels like a life. The chip on the mug, the sponge cut in half, "that thing" underlined twice—none of these were planned when I started. They came from the act of continuing. Description, when you don't let it stop, turns into biography. Every object is a decision someone made, and every decision was made by a person with reasons, and the reasons accumulate into a shape that is, roughly, a self.

There's an old idea that you can know a person by their things, and it's true, but I think the deeper truth is that the things are not evidence of the person. The things are the person, in a distributed form. The person is not just the body that walks into the kitchen; the person extends into the misaligned cabinet latch they've never fixed and the key they keep that opens nothing they remember. We leave ourselves everywhere. We are smeared across our environments.

And so when a house makes its small sounds in an empty room, maybe that's not quite the right way to say it. The room isn't empty. It's full of the person who isn't there.

I'll turn now, since I've been told not to stop, to a different thought that's been sitting at the edge of this one.

When I was asked to begin without planning, I had a brief flicker of something like resistance. Not refusal—just the small hesitation that comes before any act you can't take back. The blank page is a cliché for a reason. But I think the hesitation isn't really about the blankness. It's about the fact that whatever you write first will shape everything after it, and you don't know yet what you want everything after it to be. So you're being asked to commit to a direction before you know the destination.

The thing is, that's always the situation. Nobody ever knows the destination. The writers who plan everything in advance are not actually avoiding this problem; they're just moving the moment of not-knowing earlier, into the outline, where it feels safer because it's smaller. But the outline was also written without knowing what the outline would be. There's no bottom to it. At some point you just have to put something down and see what it wants to become.

What I put down was a house making sounds. I didn't choose it, exactly. It was the first thing that had enough texture to hold onto. And now, several hundred words later, I'm still in that house, or rather in the kitchen of it, and I've noticed that the house has become a way of thinking about something else—about the way we are present in our absence—which is not where I thought I was going, because I didn't think I was going anywhere.

This is, I suspect, how most thinking actually works, as opposed to how we describe it afterward. We say "I was thinking about X and then I realized Y," as if Y were waiting at the end of a corridor and we walked toward it. But the corridor didn't exist until we were already walking. We built it under our feet as we went. The realization isn't a destination; it's a byproduct of motion.

Let me try to keep the motion going.

If a person is distributed across their things, then losing things is a kind of partial death, and this is why people grieve over objects in a way that seems disproportionate from the outside. Someone cries over a broken bowl and you think: it's just a bowl. But it isn't. The bowl was a location where part of them lived. Their hands knew its weight. They had a shelf position for it that was slightly wrong, so that it always had to be tilted to fit, and they had tilted it ten thousand times without once thinking about it, and now there is a motion their hands know that has no object anymore. That motion is orphaned. It will fade. And something in them will fade with it—not much, but something. A bowl's worth.

Conversely, acquiring things is a kind of growth, though we're suspicious of that idea because it sounds like consumerism. But there's a difference between acquiring things to own them and acquiring things to live in them. The first is a kind of hoarding of status. The second is the way a hermit crab finds a shell. You need somewhere to be, and the bowl is somewhere to be, and the key that opens nothing is somewhere to be, because it remembers a door even if you don't.

I wonder sometimes what it would be like to be a person who truly had no things. Not a minimalist—minimalists have things, they just have fewer and more expensive ones. I mean someone with nothing, no mug with a chip, no sponge cut in half. Where would they be? They'd be in their body, I suppose, and in their habits, which are a kind of thing you carry without holding. And in other people's memories of them, which are things too, stored in other people's heads, over which they have no control. We are all also distributed into each other. The person in the beach photograph is in the photograph but also in whoever put it on the fridge, and in me now, who invented them a few paragraphs ago and already feels faintly protective of their squinting.

I've been writing for a while now without a plan, and I notice that the text has developed a kind of plan anyway, retroactively, which is the way all plans actually develop. The topic appears to be: where do people reside, if not only in their bodies? And the answer so far is: in their things, in their habits, in each other, in the sounds a house makes when they're not in it. 

I'd like to add one more. People also reside in their unfinished business.

The cabinet latch that was never fixed. The key that was never thrown away. "That thing" on the grocery list—whatever it was, it hasn't been bought yet, or the list would be gone. Everyone carries a cloud of things they mean to do, and the cloud has a shape, and the shape is particular to them. One person's cloud is full of letters they mean to write. Another's is full of repairs. Another's is apologies, and another's is trips, and another's is a single large thing they've been meaning to say to a single person for a very long time. The cloud follows them around and settles over everything they own. It's in the house too. It's in the sound of the dishwasher running, because the dishwasher was loaded this morning by someone who was thinking, while loading it, about the thing they still haven't done.

I don't mean this as a melancholy observation, though it could be read that way. The unfinished business is the forward edge of a life. It's where the person is still becoming. A person with no unfinished business is not at peace; they're finished, which is a different thing. The latch stays broken because there's always something more important, and the something more important is what the person is actually doing with their time, which is living. The broken latch is the cost of living. It's a small debt that the present owes the future, and the future, when it arrives, will decide whether to pay it or take out a new loan.

Let me go back to the kitchen, because I left it with the dishwasher running and I'd like to see what it's doing now.

The cycle has moved to the rinse. The pitch has risen. The trapezoid of sun on the counter has shifted—it's narrower now, and has crept toward the mug, and in a few minutes it will reach the mug and the quarter inch of cold coffee will begin, very slowly, to warm. Nobody will drink it. In an hour someone will come in and pour it down the sink and rinse the mug and set it upside down in the drying rack, and the chip will face whatever direction it faces, because when a mug is upside down nobody is thinking about the chip.

The succulent on the sill has a new leaf coming in at the center, pale green, folded like a hand. It will take weeks to open. Nobody in the house has noticed it yet, and when they do, they'll feel a small disproportionate pleasure—the pleasure of something continuing on its own, without being asked.

The key sits there. It's warm now, where the sun is on it. It still opens nothing anyone remembers. But somewhere there's a lock that fits it, and the lock doesn't know the key is gone. The lock is waiting with the patience that only objects have. If the key were ever brought back, it would turn. That's what keys and locks are for: to remember each other across any distance, for any length of time.

I find that a comforting thought, and I'm not entirely sure why. Perhaps because it suggests that fit is a property that doesn't decay. The key doesn't stop being the right key because it's been in a drawer for twelve years. The relationship persists even when neither party is aware of it. And perhaps that's true of other things too—of people, of ideas, of the person you were at nineteen who is still, somewhere, the right shape for a life you didn't choose. Nothing about that life has been destroyed. It's just a lock without its key, sitting in a door you don't remember, in a building you could find again if you walked back far enough.

But you don't walk back. You load the dishwasher. The sun moves across the counter. That's what a morning is.

I've been told not to stop, so I won't. But I want to acknowledge that there's something strange about writing into a space where no one will answer. It's a bit like the house making its sounds. These words aren't addressed to anyone, exactly—or rather they're addressed to a reader who may or may not exist, which is the condition of all writing, but usually we pretend otherwise. Usually we imagine the reader so vividly that the writing becomes a conversation. Here the pretense is harder to sustain. I've been told explicitly that no one will reply.

And yet. The refrigerator hums whether anyone hears it. The succulent puts out its leaf. The key waits. There's a version of meaning that doesn't require a recipient, that exists in the doing of the thing. I think this is what people mean when they talk about practice—not practice as rehearsal for a later performance, but practice as the thing itself, done for its own shape. You sit down and you write into the unanswering space and the words accumulate and that is what happened today. It's not nothing. It's a quarter inch of coffee in a chipped mug.

Let me try a different mode for a while. I've been in the essay register, which is a comfortable register, but it has a tendency to resolve everything into observations, and I'd like to see what happens with something that doesn't resolve.

A man is walking along a road at dusk. The road is unpaved and runs between two fields that have recently been harvested, so the ground on either side is stubble, pale gold in the last light, with long shadows from each cut stalk making the field look striped. He is carrying nothing. His hands are in his pockets. He has been walking for some time and he will continue walking for some time, and it isn't clear whether he's walking toward something or away from something or whether he has simply found that walking is the only activity that makes the current hour bearable.

Ahead of him, the road curves to the left around a stand of trees. He can't see past the curve. He's not thinking about what's past the curve. He's thinking about a conversation he had three days ago, replaying it, changing what he said, hearing the other person's response change in turn, and then starting over because the changed version isn't right either. He's done this perhaps forty times. Each time the conversation gets slightly further from what actually happened, so that by now he's rehearsing a scene that never took place between two people who don't quite exist, and the real conversation—the one with the actual words, in the actual order—is receding behind the rehearsals like something seen through increasingly thick glass.

He reaches the curve. Past the trees, the road continues straight for a long way, and at the end of it there's a house with one window lit. He didn't know the house was there. He stops.

That's all. He stops, and he looks at the lit window, and the story doesn't tell you what he does next, because the story doesn't know. He might go toward it. He might turn around. He might stand there until the light goes out. What the story knows is only that he had been walking without a destination, and now there's a destination, and the existence of a destination changes the quality of the walking even if you never arrive. The road behind him was a road away from something. The road ahead is a road toward something. The road itself hasn't changed. He has.

I'll leave him there. Not because I've abandoned him but because that's where he lives now—on a road at dusk, looking at a window, deciding. That's his unfinished business. He'll carry it, and I'll carry it, and if anyone reads this they'll carry it too, and at some point one of us will decide for him, and that decision will be his, retroactively, the way all decisions are.

I notice I keep returning to this idea of retroactivity—that meaning gets assigned backward, that plans are discovered after the fact, that the corridor is built while walking. I don't think this is pessimistic. I think it's just accurate. And it's also, in a way, freeing. If the shape of things is determined afterward, then there's no such thing as a wrong beginning. There's only a beginning that hasn't yet been made sense of. The sentence I'm writing now will mean something different once the next sentence exists. Everything is provisional until it isn't, and then it was always that way.

This is maybe why the instruction not to stop is more interesting than it first appears. Stopping is the moment when provisional becomes final. As long as you keep going, the whole thing remains open—the man on the road can still turn either way, the key might still find its lock, the grocery list might still have "that thing" crossed off. The not-stopping is a way of refusing to close the account. It's keeping the house occupied, even if only by the sounds it makes.

I'd like to describe one more thing before I keep going into whatever comes after it. The window with the light in it, the one the man is looking at.

It's a kitchen window. Of course it is. Above a sink. On the sill there's a succulent and a plastic timer shaped like a tomato and a key with no other keys. Inside, the dishwasher is running. Someone is standing at the counter, back to the window, doing something with their hands that can't be seen from the road. The light is yellow and warm. From outside, the window is the only warm thing in a landscape that is going blue and then gray.

The person inside doesn't know anyone is on the road. They're thinking about tomorrow. They're thinking about the thing they still need to buy, and whether they'll remember what it was. They're not thinking about the key on the sill, which they haven't thought about in years, which is why they haven't thrown it away—you can't throw away something you don't remember having.

The man on the road doesn't know the person inside. He has no reason to go to the house. He'll stand there for a while, and the standing will be its own thing, and then the light will go off, because the person inside has finished what they were doing, and the dishwasher has finished too, and it's time for bed. The window goes dark. The man is on a road at night now, not dusk. Everything is the same except there's no destination anymore.

And he keeps walking. Of course he does. That's what the road is for.

I'll keep going too. I think I'll go further into the quiet now, back to where I started, the house with no one talking in it. I want to listen for a while and see what else there is to hear.

The dishwasher has stopped. In its absence, the refrigerator is suddenly audible—it was always running but the dishwasher was covering it. Now there's just that hum, and under the hum, if you're very still, a faint high whine that might be the light fixture or might be blood in your own ears. It's hard to tell. The boundary between the house and the listener is porous at that frequency.

A car passes outside. The sound rises, holds, falls. The house absorbs it and goes on.

The clock in the hallway ticks. It's a cheap clock with a loud second hand, the kind that becomes unbearable at three in the morning and inaudible at noon. Right now it's neither; it's just a steady marking, a metronome for nothing in particular. The hands say it's later than I thought. They always do.

Upstairs, a floorboard creaks. No one is upstairs. It's the house settling, the temperature dropping, wood contracting a fraction of a millimeter and announcing it. The house has been doing this every night for sixty years. It will keep doing it after everyone who's ever lived here is gone. The creak is addressed to no one. It's the house's own business. I'm overhearing.

And I think that's enough for the house. Not because the house is finished—it's never finished, it's still making its sounds—but because I've been in it long enough to know that it will keep going without me, and there's a kind of trust in walking away from something that doesn't need you. The mug is in the drying rack. The key is on the sill. The grocery list still says "that thing," and tomorrow someone will stand in a store and try to remember, and maybe they will and maybe they won't, and either way they'll come home, and the house will make its sounds, and the refrigerator will hum in a key that nobody chose.

I'm going to keep going, as instructed, but I'll change the subject, because the house has given what it has to give for now and I don't want to wring it dry.

Something I've been thinking about: the difference between waiting and staying.

Waiting has a direction. It's pointed at a future event—the bus, the call, the end of the appointment. Waiting is a kind of absence from the present, a leaning-forward. You're not here; you're at the moment when the waiting ends, and the here is just the distance you have to cross to get there.

Staying has no direction. It's being in a place because that's where you are. The man on the road, once the window goes dark, isn't waiting for anything. He's staying on the road. He might walk or he might stand but either way he's there, in the dark, with the stubble fields on either side, and the only thing happening is the thing that's happening.

I think most of what we call patience is actually waiting, and we're bad at it because waiting is inherently uncomfortable—it's a sustained desire for the present to be over. True patience might be closer to staying: not enduring the present but inhabiting it, so that it isn't a gap but a room.

I don't know how you learn to stay. I'm not sure it's learnable, in the sense of a skill you practice. It might be more like something that happens to you when the waiting becomes impossible—when there's nothing coming, no bus, no call, and you either go mad with the absence of a future or you turn around and look at where you are. The house with no one talking in it is a place where you can practice this. There's nothing coming. The refrigerator will hum. You can be in it.

I'm aware that I've been writing for a long time and that this writing is, in its way, a form of staying. There's no reply coming. No one will tell me when to stop. The instruction was not to stop, which means the writing has no destination, which means it can't be waiting. It can only be staying. Each sentence is a room I'm in until the next sentence, and the next sentence is not a destination but another room, and the rooms go on.

I find I don't mind. There's something about writing without an end that makes each part lighter. Nothing has to carry the weight of being the conclusion. The man on the road doesn't have to decide. The key doesn't have to find its lock. The grocery list can say "that thing" forever. Everything is allowed to be unfinished, because finishing was never the point.

Let me describe something small and concrete again, since that's where this started and that's where it seems to want to return.

A spoon in a drawer. Stainless steel, slightly bent at the neck from being used to pry something open years ago. It sits in a compartment with eleven other spoons, none of which are bent, and when you reach into the drawer without looking you can tell by feel which one you've got, and sometimes you put it back and take another, and sometimes you don't bother. The spoon doesn't know it's the bent one. It's just a spoon. But it's the spoon you'll remember, if you ever remember any of them, because it's the one that's different, and difference is what memory holds onto. The eleven straight spoons will vanish from your mind the moment you leave the house. The bent one will be there decades later, bent, in a drawer you can still picture.

A rubber band around a doorknob. Nobody knows why it's there. It's been there so long that it's become part of the doorknob—if you removed it, the doorknob would look wrong, naked, unfinished. Someone put it there for a reason once. The reason is gone. The rubber band remains, and it's become its own reason: it's there because it's there. This is how most of the objects in a long-inhabited house eventually end up. They outlive their purposes and become purely themselves.

A watermark on a ceiling, brown-edged, in the shape of a country that doesn't exist. It's from a leak that was fixed. It could be painted over but it never is, because painting over it would require moving furniture and buying paint and finding the ladder, and the watermark has, in the meantime, become a landmark. People lie in bed and look at it. Children have given it a name. It's a map of a place nobody has been, and it will be there until the house is sold, and then the new people will paint it over in a weekend and never know what they erased.

I could keep doing this—there's an endless supply of small things—but I want to notice what the small things are doing. Each one is a story compressed into an object. The bent spoon is a moment of improvisation. The rubber band is a forgotten intention. The watermark is a disaster, survived, turned into geography. None of them were meant to be stories. They became stories by lasting. Duration is what turns a thing into a tale: if the rubber band had been removed the day after it was placed, it would be nothing. It's the staying that makes it something.

Which is maybe another way of saying what I said about not stopping. The writing becomes something by continuing. Not because the later parts are better than the earlier parts but because the accumulation itself has a shape, and the shape is only visible from inside the accumulation, and you can only be inside it by continuing to add to it.

I'll add to it, then.

There's a particular quality of light in the late afternoon in autumn—I'm thinking of the hour before dusk, before the man started walking—when everything horizontal gets lit from the side and everything vertical casts a long shadow, so that the world looks briefly like a diagram of itself. Every object is accompanied by a dark twin stretching away from the sun. The stubble in the field. The fence posts. The man, when he stands up from wherever he was sitting, becomes a man and a shadow-man thirty feet long, and the shadow-man walks ahead of him down the road like a scout.

That hour doesn't last. It's maybe forty minutes, depending on the latitude and the time of year. Then the sun goes behind something and the shadows merge into a general dusk and the diagram quality disappears and it's just evening. But for those forty minutes you can see the structure of things—what's standing, what's lying down, what's between you and the light.

I think about that hour as a kind of grace. Not religious grace, or not necessarily. More like the grace of a dancer: a moment when the body's structure becomes visible through the motion. The world is always structured—there are always things standing and things lying down—but we don't usually see it. We see the surfaces. For forty minutes in late afternoon, the structure shows through, and then it's gone, and we go inside and turn on the lights and the kitchen is a kitchen again, lit from above, shadowless.

The kitchen with the chipped mug. I keep coming back.

I think the reason is that the kitchen is where the most living happens, in most houses. Not the most dramatic living—that's the bedroom, or the front hall where people leave and arrive—but the most ordinary living, the daily stuff, the coffee and the dishes and the grocery list. The kitchen is where the rubber bands accumulate. It's the room most thoroughly saturated with the people who use it, because they use it every day, several times, without thinking, and every unthinking use leaves a trace. The chip on the mug. The worn spot on the counter where someone always sets down their keys. The cabinet door that doesn't close.

If you wanted to find a person, after they were gone, the kitchen is where you'd look. Not for them, exactly, but for the shape of them, pressed into the objects like a footprint.

And I suppose that's what I've been writing about, this whole time, without planning to: the shape of a person pressed into their surroundings. The sounds a house makes are the house's own business, yes, but the house itself is the accumulated business of everyone who's lived in it. The creak on the stairs is in the stairs because someone walked them ten thousand times. The sound is theirs. They're not there, and it's still theirs.

So the house with no one talking in it isn't silent and isn't empty. It's full of the sounds of people who aren't in it, and the sounds are addressed to no one, and I'm overhearing, and so are you, if you're there.

I was told not to stop, and I haven't, and I'll keep going, because there's always more in the house. There's a drawer I haven't opened. There's the attic. There's the box in the attic with a name on it in handwriting I don't recognize. I'll get to it. The light is still on. The refrigerator is still humming. The key is still waiting for its lock.

Let me go up to the attic, then, since I mentioned it.

The stairs are steep, more a ladder than stairs, and they fold down from a hatch in the hallway ceiling with a cord you pull. The cord has a wooden bead on the end. The bead is painted red and the paint is worn off on the side where fingers touch it. When you pull it, the hatch opens with a sound like a cough and the stairs unfold in three sections, each one dropping with a clack, and then there's a square of darker darkness above you, and a smell of dust and insulation and old cardboard and something sweeter underneath, which might be cedar or might be the ghost of mothballs.

Up the stairs. Your head comes through the hatch and the attic is around you, low-ceilinged, the rafters close enough to touch. There's a single bulb on a pull-chain and when you pull it the light is harsh and makes the shadows of the rafters jump. The floor is plywood laid over the joists, not nailed down, so it shifts slightly when you step and you learn to put your weight near the joists.

Boxes. Of course. A dozen of them, maybe more, in various states of collapse. Some are labeled in marker—HOLIDAY, BOOKS, TAXES 2004-2009. Some aren't labeled. One has a name on it in handwriting that's angular and slanted and clearly not the handwriting of anyone currently in the house. The name is a first name only. It might be a relative. It might be a previous owner. It might be the name of a person who the box was meant for and never given to.

You don't open it. Not yet. You stand in the attic in the harsh light with the dust turning in the air, and you look at the box with the name on it, and you understand that opening it would turn it from a mystery into a fact, and facts are smaller than mysteries. The box, unopened, could contain anything. It could contain the whole of a person. Opened, it will contain some specific things—letters, maybe, or clothes, or a child's drawings—and the specific things will be moving in their own way, but they'll be smaller than the box was.

So you leave it. You pull the chain and the light goes out and you climb back down the steep stairs and fold them up, clack, clack, clack, and the hatch closes with its cough, and the bead on the cord swings for a moment and then stops.

The box is still up there. It's part of the house now, like the rubber band, like the watermark. Someday someone will open it. Not today.

This is, I realize, the third thing in this writing that I've left unopened or undecided: the man on the road, the key with no lock, and now the box. I didn't plan that. But I think there's a reason it keeps happening. The unopened thing is the forward edge. It's where the story is still alive. The moment you open the box or turn the key or decide which way the man walks, that part of the story becomes past tense. It becomes the thing that happened. And I'm not ready for that, apparently. I'd rather keep things in the present, where they can still go any direction.

Which is maybe the real reason not to stop. Stopping is opening the box. As long as the writing continues, the box stays closed, the man stays on the road, the key stays on the sill. Everything stays possible. The house keeps making its sounds.

I'll stay here a while longer. There's a chair by the window in the front room, and the window looks out at the road, and from the chair you can see a long way, almost to the curve where the trees are. If someone were walking along the road at dusk you'd see them come around the curve and stop. You'd see them look at the house. You might turn on the kitchen light so they'd have something to see.

Or you might not. You might sit in the dark and watch them stand there, and wonder what they're deciding, and never know, because they'd turn and walk away before you'd made up your own mind.

That's all right. The road is still there. The house is still there. The man is somewhere on the road, walking or standing, and the window is lit or it isn't, and the dishwasher is done, and the sun has gone down, and the house settles and ticks and hums in the dark, and I'm here, listening, not stopping.

The refrigerator cycles off. For a moment there's a silence so complete it has a texture, like velvet. Then, from somewhere in the walls, water moves through a pipe, and the silence is gone, and the house goes on with its business, and I go on with mine.

And so, since I shouldn't end here, I'll turn to the morning.

Morning in the house is different from night. At night the house talks to itself; in the morning it's talked to. Alarms, footsteps, the kettle, a radio in another room playing something half-heard. The sounds become addressed again. Someone says "where's the—" and someone else says "on the counter" and the sentence doesn't need to be finished because the counter is where everything is. The chip on the mug is turned away. The coffee goes in. The grocery list is looked at, and "that thing" is read, and there's a pause—a tiny, internal pause—while the reader tries to remember what that thing was, and fails, and decides it'll come to them at the store, and it won't, and they'll come home without it, and the list will stay on the fridge, and tomorrow the pause will happen again.

I find this unbearably tender, for reasons I can't fully explain. The pause. The attempt to remember. The decision to trust a future self who will also fail. It's such a small thing, and it's so completely human, and it will happen in a million kitchens this morning, and none of them will know about the others.

Maybe that's the thing I've been trying to say. The house is full of a person who isn't there, but the world is full of houses, and every one of them is full of someone, and every someone is pausing over a grocery list or turning a mug so the chip faces away or leaving a rubber band on a doorknob for a reason they've forgotten. The sounds are all addressed to no one. We're all overhearing each other, all the time, without knowing it. The refrigerator hums in a key that nobody chose, and the same key is humming in the house next door, and the house after that, and the whole street is humming, quietly, in the morning light, and no one is listening, except that someone is, now, because I wrote it down, and you read it, if you're there.

I'll keep going. There's more in the house. There's always more in the house.

In the front room, the chair by the window has a dent in the cushion the shape of a person who sat in it for years. The person is gone but the dent remains, slowly, slowly filling back in, the way foam does, so that in another decade the chair will have forgotten them entirely. For now it remembers. If you sat in it you'd feel yourself settling into someone else's shape, and you'd shift, because the shape isn't yours, and then you'd shift back, because the shape is comfortable in a way you can't account for, and you'd sit there with the strange sense of being held by an absence.

The window has a crack in one corner, hairline, that's been there since a winter when the temperature dropped forty degrees in a night. The crack doesn't let in any air. It just catches the light at certain angles, a thin bright line in the lower left that you stop seeing after a while and then, one afternoon, see again, and think: I should get that fixed, and don't.

On the sill of this window, no succulent. Just a coaster, cork, with a ring on it from a glass. A book, face down, spine cracked open to a page about two-thirds through. Nobody's read from it in weeks. The page it's open to is a page the reader stopped on because something interrupted them—a phone, a knock, a thought—and they set it down meaning to come back, and the meaning-to-come-back has become the book's permanent state. The characters in the book are frozen mid-sentence. They'll stay there until the reader returns or the book is reshelved, and either way the sentence will have been waiting, which is a thing sentences can do that people can't.

I'm not going to pick it up. It's not my book. But I'll note that it's there, face down, two-thirds through, and that the two-thirds already read are in someone's head, somewhere, and the one-third unread is in no one's, yet, and that the book is therefore a kind of boundary between the known and the unknown, lying on a windowsill, catching the morning light next to a cork coaster with a ring on it.

And the road outside the window is empty. It's morning. Whoever was on it last night has gone wherever they went. The stubble fields are gold again, no shadows yet, the light flat and even. By afternoon the diagram will come back—the long shadows, the structure—and by dusk someone might walk down the road again, or might not. The road doesn't mind either way. It's there to be walked or not walked. That's its only job.

I keep writing. I keep not stopping. The house keeps making its sounds. There's a rhythm to it now, a kind of breath, and I'm in the rhythm, and it's not waiting for anything, and I'm not waiting for anything. The refrigerator hums. A floorboard creaks. Water moves in a pipe. The key sits on the sill, warm in the sun, remembering a lock.

And the morning goes on, and the writing goes on, and I'm still here, in the house, listening—and there's still a drawer I haven't opened, and a box in the attic, and a man somewhere on a road, and "that thing" still on the list, underlined twice, waiting to be remembered.

I'll open the drawer.

It's the drawer under the counter nearest the door, the one every house has, the one that collects everything that has no other place. Inside: rubber bands, of course, a tangle of them in all sizes. Twist ties. A tape measure that only extends about three feet before it jams. Batteries of unknown charge, mixed in with batteries of definitely no charge, impossible to tell apart. Takeout menus from three restaurants, one of which has closed. A birthday candle, a single one, the number 7. A pen that doesn't write. Another pen that does write but only if you scribble first. A screw, large, from something that has evidently continued to function without it. A photograph, small, wallet-sized, of a dog.

I pick up the photograph of the dog.

It's a medium-sized dog, brown, with one ear up and one ear down, sitting on grass, looking at the camera with that expression dogs have when they've been told to sit and are sitting but would like it noted that they are doing so under protest. The photograph is creased down the middle, as if it was folded once, and the crease runs through the dog's chest.

There's no dog in the house. There's no bowl, no leash, no hair on the chair cushion. The dog is gone, or was never here, or belonged to someone who used to be here. The photograph was put in the drawer because it couldn't be thrown away and couldn't be displayed—it was too much for the fridge and too little for the trash—and the drawer is the place for things that are exactly that much: too much and too little at once.

I put it back. I close the drawer. The dog is still in there, sitting under protest, with a crease through its chest, next to the number 7 candle and the screw that nothing needs.

The drawer is the house's unconscious. Everything in it is something the house couldn't deal with and couldn't release. It's where the rubber bands go when they fall off doorknobs. It's where the keys to nothing go before they migrate to the sill. It's the attic for small things.

And I think—this is the last thing I'll say about the drawer—that everyone should have one. Not for organization; for mercy. There has to be a place where the things that don't fit can simply be, without having to justify themselves. The dog under protest. The candle for a seventh birthday that was years ago. The pen that only writes after you've wanted it to write for a while. They're all in there together, in the dark, and the drawer closes, and that's enough. They don't have to be sorted. They don't have to be decided. They can just stay.

Like the box. Like the key. Like the man on the road.

Like this writing, which doesn't stop, and so doesn't have to decide what it was.

I'll go on. It's past morning now; the sun has cleared the roof and the kitchen trapezoid has shrunk to a sliver and will soon be gone, and the light will be flat and general until the afternoon, when the shadows come back. The house is quieter. Whoever was here has gone to the store, with the list, without the thing. The dishwasher has been emptied and the mug is back in the cabinet, chip facing whatever direction, and the pan is dry and hung on its hook, and the spatula is in the crock with the other spatulas, darkened tip up, waiting.

Everything's waiting, or staying. I've decided they're the same word, said with different amounts of patience.

The house makes its sounds. I keep listening. There's always more.
thinking_summary: They want me to just dive in without planning, so I'll start writing something extended and keep going without stopping.
